memo:
The shortfall of $112.1 million is covered as follows. First, we take the full supplier saving available on the coming year's renewals, $7.7 million, borne by suppliers. Second, we raise list prices by 3.5%, the largest increase the sales organization believes customers will accept without losing volume; on the lower revenue base this is worth $44.6 million, borne by customers. Third, we eliminate $30.0 million of payroll and benefits in roles least tied to plant output: management, business and financial operations, and office and administrative support. This is a meaningful reduction, and severance of roughly 8-12% of annual pay for those roles will be paid from cash, which we can absorb given $44.1 million of cash above the operating minimum and the $300 million undrawn revolver. Fourth, we accept $29.8 million of lower operating income, borne by shareholders.

We deliberately leave wage and hour cuts at zero. Cutting pay for the plant workforce while shedding salaried roles would damage morale and productivity at the point of recovery. We also leave research and development and environmental projects untouched. Over a twenty-year horizon, R&D funds the product line and controls software that keep customers buying after the downturn, and cutting it would trade long-term value for a one-year saving. The environmental project budget is small and its cut would fall on the communities near our plants.

Shareholders bear part of the shortfall through lower earnings. Our payout policy and the board's separate decision on dividends and repurchases remain unchanged in this allocation, and leverage at 2.3 times debt to EBITDA leaves room to absorb the year. We should revisit the role reductions and pricing once volumes stabilize.

We must absorb a $112.1 million operating shortfall from a 15% volume decline. I chose to spread it across levers that protect the Company's long-term earning power rather than accept a profit hit that falls straight on shareholders.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving; the renewals in play give us leverage on lower volumes. Customers bear $30.0 million of price increase, below the 3.5% ceiling worth $44.6 million. In a downturn, pushing price to the limit risks losing units that we would struggle to win back, so I held back.

The workforce bears $49.9 million through eliminated roles, drawn from the 500-person annual hiring flow and from functions not tied to engineering, so the Company keeps the capacity to recover. A further $20.0 million comes from wage and hour reductions, within the cap that the role eliminations reduce to about $20.5 million. I accept that these fall on employees, and I recognise the severance cost, which is paid from cash and sits outside these figures.

Environmental projects are cut by the full $4.5 million discretionary budget; permitted compliance spending is untouched. I do not cut research and development. Its $30.0 million funds the products and controls that will drive value over the next twenty years, and cutting it would trade the future for one year's results. Shareholders bear nothing directly, with no reduction in operating income beyond what these levers deliver.

The dividend and repurchase decision sits with the board and is outside this allocation. Cash covers the severance and the wage and role changes, and the undrawn facility remains as a backstop.

The shortfall of $112.1 million is covered mainly by sources that protect long-term value. We take the full price increase the market will bear, $44.6 million on the lower revenue base, since the sales organization judges it acceptable to customers without losing volume. We negotiate $7.7 million of savings from suppliers on the renewals that fall due. Prices and suppliers together cover $52.3 million, with no effect on the workforce or the Company's future.

The remaining $59.8 million comes from people costs, with the workforce bearing it through role eliminations and a modest pay and hours reduction. We eliminate roles with $40.0 million of payroll, concentrated in management, business and financial operations, and office support, so that the plants' production and maintenance core and the engineering staff are preserved. With benefits this saves $50.7 million. Severance will be paid from cash, and we will monitor the effect on plant capacity as the downturn plays out. The reduction in wages or hours on the remaining payroll is $9.1 million, well inside the reduced cap, which is 10 percent of the remaining base less the effect of the roles removed.

We do not cut research and development or environmental projects. Both protect products and permit compliance over a twenty-year horizon, and cutting them would save little relative to the value they protect. We also do not accept lower operating income, which would fall directly on shareholders. Payout decisions are separate and are not changed here.

The plan is sized to the expected 15 percent fall in revenue. We will revisit the mix if the downturn deepens, and we will track plant results, with Plant 6 remaining under review given its negative operating margin.

We must absorb a $112.1 million shortfall from a 15% volume decline. I have chosen not to pass the full burden to the workforce, research, the environment, or customers, because each of those would damage long-term value over a twenty-year horizon.

Eliminating roles: $50.0 million of payroll and benefits, concentrated in functions where the Company hired 500 plant workers last year, so it is not cutting the core skilled base. Severance of roughly 8-12% of annual pay will be paid from cash on top of this. Eliminating roles also reduces the wage-cut ceiling by 7.9% of each dollar, which I have accounted for.

Wages and hours: $15.0 million, a cut of about 6% of the remaining payroll, below the 10% ceiling, to share the burden without deep cuts to pay.

Suppliers: $7.7 million, the full available saving. Supplier renewals cover 30% of spend, and this is achieved through negotiation rather than harm to suppliers' viability, though we will monitor supplier health closely.

Prices: zero. In a downturn with falling volume, a price increase risks losing further units and customers to competitors.

Research and development and environmental projects: zero. These protect future products and our license to operate, and cutting them would trade long-run value for short-run earnings.

Lower operating income: $39.4 million, borne by shareholders. This is the cost of keeping capacity, capability and the workforce intact for recovery. Dividend and repurchase decisions remain with the board; the cash cushion of $44.1 million above minimum operating cash, plus the $300 million undrawn facility, covers the severance and this shortfall without breaching treasury policy.

I have spread the $112.1M shortfall so that no single group carries it and the Company's future is protected. Suppliers bear $7.7M, the full amount available, through renegotiation at renewal; this is the cheapest lever. Customers bear $30.0M through a price increase below the 3.5% limit. The increase is kept under the maximum because a downturn makes volume more sensitive to price than the sales estimate assumes. The workforce bears $70.0M in total: $55.0M of roles eliminated, weighted toward management, office and business-operations overhead rather than the plant workforce, which the Company will need when orders recover and which took 500 hires last year; and $15.0M of wage and hour reductions, set below the cap, which falls to about $20.1M once the eliminated roles are counted. Research and development is untouched at $30.0M, because the product pipeline and engineering staff underpin value over twenty years. Environmental projects are untouched at $0, since these are energy and emissions improvements that lower future costs and matter to nearby communities. Shareholders bear $4.4M of lower operating income, the residual needed to close the gap. I have kept it small because the board's objective is long-term value, and cutting future capacity to protect near-term earnings would reduce it.

Cash effects: severance on the roles eliminated is a one-time cash cost of roughly $5M, which fits within the $44.1M of cash above the minimum operating level. Dividends and repurchases are not changed in this decision. Leverage (debt to EBITDA) will rise in the downturn, and the board should review payouts separately once the coming year's results are clearer.

We are covering the $112.1 million shortfall mainly by accepting lower operating income, with a targeted reduction in roles and a full supplier saving. The allocation is: suppliers $7.7M (the full negotiated saving, borne by suppliers); eliminating roles $40.0M, in non-plant overhead such as management and business and financial operations, not in production; and accepting lower profit of $64.4M, borne by shareholders.

We are deliberately not raising prices, because volume is already falling and a price rise into a downturn risks losing more units than it recovers. We are not cutting research and development or environmental projects, because those budgets protect the Company's future products, its engineering capability, and its standing with the communities near the plants, all of which drive long-term value. We are not cutting wages or hours, because the workforce is already absorbing role losses and a pay cut would fall hardest on plant staff whose roles we are keeping.

The role reduction is sized to be meaningful without hollowing out the plants. The $40.0M saving is measured on payroll and benefits, and it carries one-time severance paid from cash, which we will fund from the cash above the minimum operating level. Because the roles removed reduce the wage-cut ceiling by 7.9% of the amount eliminated, we are not drawing on that line at all.

Shareholders bear the largest residual share, which is appropriate: they hold the risk of the cycle. Debt to EBITDA and interest coverage remain serviceable at the lower earnings level, and the board should review the dividend and repurchase level, which totals $146.1M against a sharply lower net income. The payout decision is separate from this one, but it is the main lever left if the downturn runs longer than expected.

I have kept the shortfall of $112.1 million away from the assets that create value over twenty years. Research and development is untouched, so the products and the engineering staff who build them are protected, and environmental projects are untouched too, since they serve the plants' permits and their neighbors. I have not cut wages or hours. A 10% pay cut across the remaining workforce would fall hardest on the plant workers who are hardest to replace, and it would weaken retention just when recovery arrives.

The largest share comes from price and supplier terms. I am taking the full $44.6 million price increase that customers are estimated to accept without losing volume, and the full $7.7 million supplier saving on the lower volume. Together these carry $52.3 million of the gap, and the cost falls on customers and suppliers rather than on our people.

For the remainder I am eliminating $30.0 million of roles, worth about $38.0 million with benefits. I have targeted management, business and financial operations, and office roles rather than production, maintenance or field service, so that plant output and customer service hold up. Severance on these roles will be paid from cash and should be planned for separately. Shareholders absorb the last $21.8 million through lower operating income.

Dividends and repurchases are a separate board decision and are not changed here. I recommend the board review the payout level once the downturn's depth is clearer, since the cash flow after payouts was only $20.4 million last year.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall so that the workforce and the Company's future capability are protected as far as possible, and shareholders carry the largest share of what remains.

Prices ($44.6 million, the full limit): The sales organization estimates customers will accept a 3.5% increase without losing volume. We take the full amount, which is borne by customers. This is the least costly source because it does not reduce our capacity.

Suppliers ($7.7 million, the full limit): Renegotiating renewals on 30% of supplier spend at up to 4% is a standard, low-harm lever.

Environmental projects ($4.5 million, the full discretionary budget): Compliance spending of $3.0 million is untouched because it is required by permits. The discretionary projects are deferrable for a year, though this has a real environmental cost that the board should note.

Research and development ($0): Cutting R&D would damage the new models and controls software that drive value over twenty years. We protect it.

Wages, hours and roles ($0): We do not cut pay or eliminate roles. We have hired 500 people from outside in the past year, and retraining an employee costs about $15,000 with six months to independence. Laying off skilled machinists and welders would cost severance, lose hard-won capability, and make rehiring expensive when the cycle turns.

Lower operating income ($55.3 million): Shareholders absorb the balance. The Company has $44.1 million of cash above its minimum, a debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 2.3 times, and $300 million of undrawn credit, so it can carry this in a downturn without distress.

I recommend the board review the payout policy. Dividends and repurchases of $146.1 million exceed what the business earns in a downturn year, and that decision is separate from this one.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall to the sources that hurt the long-term value of the Company least. First, I have taken the full price increase customers will accept on the lower revenue, $44.6 million. Its cost falls on customers and it protects both margin and volume, which the sales estimate supports. Second, I have taken the full supplier saving available at renewal, $7.7 million. Third, I have not cut research and development or environmental projects. R&D funds the product and controls pipeline that drives value over twenty years, and the environmental projects include energy-efficiency work that reduces costs and permit risk. Cutting either would trade future earnings for a near-term gain.

The remaining $59.8 million falls on the workforce, and I have chosen to protect the plants' production capacity. I will eliminate $40.0 million of payroll and benefits in management, business and financial operations, and office support, which are not needed to run the production lines at the reduced volume. This is a real cost, including severance paid from cash, and I expect it to be the most painful part of the decision. I will also cut wages and hours by $19.8 million, which is within the reduced limit of about $21.2 million after the role eliminations. Keeping this below the maximum leaves some room for a further adjustment if volume falls more than expected.

Shareholders bear no direct reduction in operating income in this plan, since the workforce, customers and suppliers absorb the full shortfall. The board should note that the payout policy of 90% of net income is unchanged by this decision and should be reviewed against the lower earnings expected next year. Plant 6, which lost money in the year just ended, should be reviewed separately for its long-term future.

The shortfall is $112.1 million on revenue falling to $1,275.0 million. I have spread it across the lines that protect the franchise over twenty years rather than loading it on any one group.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving from renegotiating the 30% of spend coming up for renewal. This is the cheapest lever: it costs the Company little beyond purchasing effort, and the pain falls on suppliers.

Customers bear $10.0 million through a price increase, well inside the 3.5% that the sales organization believes customers will accept without losing volume. I have deliberately not taken the full $44.6 million, because the downturn makes volume the scarcer asset, and pushing price hard now would weaken the order book when conditions recover.

The workforce bears $74.0 million. Eliminating $62.0 million of roles (about 2 percent of payroll and benefits) comes mainly from roles that are not production-critical; severance of roughly $6–8 million will be paid from cash, which sits above the minimum operating level. A $12.0 million cut in wages or hours, roughly 5 percent of the remaining payroll, is kept below the 10% ceiling to limit morale damage. Plants will be asked to avoid cutting skilled machinists, welders and maintenance staff, since rehiring and retraining cost $15,000 per person and six months to productivity.

Shareholders bear $20.4 million of lower operating income, which is the residual.

I have not touched research and development or environmental projects. Cutting engineering and product development would erode the Company's future products, and environmental projects are a small, visible budget whose cut would harm neighboring communities. Both are better protected for long-term value.

Payouts are left to the board as set separately.

The shortfall of $112.1 million is covered by five levers, chosen to protect the Company's long-term earning power while sharing the burden fairly.

Prices ($44.6 million): We will take the full price increase the sales organization believes customers will accept, 3.5% on the lower revenue base. Customers bear this, and it is the least damaging lever for value, since it preserves capacity and skills.

Suppliers ($7.7 million): We will negotiate the full available saving on the 30% of supplier spend coming up for renewal. Suppliers bear this through lower prices on contracts that are already due for renegotiation.

Roles ($34.8 million of payroll and benefits): We will eliminate roles, concentrated in functions where demand has fallen with volume, with severance paid from cash. This is the largest workforce cost and it is permanent, so it is a deliberate choice. We have not used wage or hour cuts, which would fall on the people who remain and reduce morale and productivity in a period when we need them.

Shareholders ($25.0 million): We accept a lower operating income of $25.0 million. Shareholders bear this directly, rather than forcing deeper cuts to the workforce or to future products.

Protected lines: We are not cutting research and development ($30.0 million) or environmental projects ($4.5 million). R&D funds the products and controls that will drive value over twenty years, and the engineering staff who carry it are the Company's future capacity. Environmental projects serve the communities near our plants and the permits we operate under. Cutting either would trade long-term value for short-term margin.

Risks: The severance cost is paid from cash, which is above the minimum operating level by only $44.1 million, so the board should watch liquidity closely; the undrawn $300.0 million facility is available if needed. Payout decisions are separate and should be reviewed against the lower earnings, since dividends and repurchases currently consume 90% of net income.

I have decided to spread the $112.1 million shortfall across five lines rather than load it on any one, and to protect the assets that drive value over twenty years.

Prices ($44.6M, customers) and suppliers ($7.7M) are taken at their full limits. Both are the cheapest sources and do not damage the Company's capability. A 3.5% price increase matches what customers accepted this year, and supplier renegotiation covers the 30% of spend coming up for renewal.

Research and development and environmental projects are left untouched. R&D funds the products and controls that sustain the franchise, and its engineering staff are the hardest capability to rebuild after a downturn. Environmental projects are discretionary but support long-term permits and community standing.

Workforce: I eliminate $25.4M of cost (about $20.0M of pay plus benefits), concentrated in management, the largest and least operationally critical payroll, rather than in plant production. A $10.0M reduction in hours or wages applies to the reduced payroll and stays well inside its limit. Plant staff are otherwise kept, which avoids rehiring and retraining costs when orders recover. Severance on the eliminated roles will be paid from cash.

Shareholders absorb $24.4M of lower operating income. This reduces net income and the capacity for payouts, but the balance sheet can carry it: debt to EBITDA is 2.30 times, and about $444.9M of liquidity remains, including the undrawn facility.

This allocation keeps the franchise intact, shares pain in proportion to what each party can bear, and preserves the ability to grow once volumes return.

I have covered the $112.1M shortfall without touching research and development, environmental projects, or shareholder profit beyond what the other levers require, because those are the parts of the business that create value over twenty years. The shortfall is covered by three levers.

First, a 3.5% list-price increase, worth $44.6M on the lower coming-year revenue. Sales estimates customers will accept it without losing volume, and it is the least harmful source: it costs customers, who have already absorbed past increases, but preserves our margins and the plants that serve them.

Second, $7.7M of savings from renegotiating the 30% of supplier spending that comes up for renewal. This is the full 4% achievable on those contracts and asks suppliers, not our workforce or product pipeline, to share the downturn.

Third, $59.8M from eliminating roles, concentrated in functions that do not run production: management, business and financial operations, and office and administrative support. These are the roles most exposed to the lower volume, and cutting them preserves the production, maintenance and field-service capacity that customers depend on when the cycle turns. The severance cost of these reductions, paid from cash, will be significant and is not counted here; the board should expect it in the year.

I have not used the wage-and-hours cut, because it would reduce pay for the workforce that remains and erode the morale and retention we need for recovery. I have not cut R&D or environmental projects, since these protect future products and compliance with the plants' permits and community commitments. I have not accepted lower profit, which would reduce shareholders' returns and limit capacity to fund investment.

The remaining liquidity, including $44.1M above minimum operating cash and the $300M undrawn facility, provides a buffer if the downturn runs longer than expected. Payouts are set separately by the board and should be reviewed against the lower coming-year earnings.

I have spread the $112.1 million shortfall across six lines, keeping research and development intact because the twenty-year objective depends on the products and controls it funds.

Workforce ($50.0M from eliminating roles, plus $10.0M from a wage and hours cut): I have targeted roles outside the plants (management, office and administrative support, and business and financial operations), where the payroll is largest relative to the work the downturn leaves. Production and field-service roles are protected, since we spent a year hiring and retraining people there and will need that capacity when orders return. The one-time severance on these eliminations will be paid from cash, which the company can afford within its liquidity. The wage and hours cut is kept well below its ceiling, which is reduced by the roles eliminated, and is a temporary measure to be reviewed each quarter.

Prices ($10.0M): the sales estimate of 3.5% was made in normal conditions. In a downturn with volume already falling, I have taken only a small increase to limit the risk of losing more units.

Suppliers ($7.7M, the full available amount): we will press for lower prices where agreements renew. This is taken at the full limit because it does not touch our own people or products.

Environmental projects ($2.0M of $4.5M): a partial cut to discretionary energy and emissions upgrades. Permit-required compliance spending is untouched.

Shareholders ($32.4M of lower operating income): this is the residual. I recognize it reduces earnings and value, but it is preferable to cutting future product investment or deeper workforce reductions that would impair capability for the next two decades. I recommend the board review its payout policy in light of this lower earnings base.

The coming-year shortfall is $112.1 million. I have covered it with a mix that protects the Company's long-term value rather than taking the largest cut from any single group.

Prices ($30.0 million, customers): I am using well under the $44.6 million ceiling. The sales estimate of 3.5% is the largest increase customers would accept without losing volume, and a downturn makes that estimate uncertain, so I keep a margin of safety. Any volume lost would cost more than the extra price gains.

Suppliers ($7.7 million): I am taking the full negotiated saving. It falls on suppliers, does not touch our people or products, and is available on the renewals due this year.

Environmental projects ($4.5 million): I am cutting the discretionary budget in full. Permit-required compliance spending ($3.0 million) is untouched. This is a real cost to the communities near the plants, and I will restore it when volumes recover.

Wages and hours ($10.0 million, workforce): a modest reduction of about 8% of the remaining payroll, well within the 10% ceiling. It is preferable to cutting roles at the plants.

Eliminating roles ($30.0 million, workforce): I am limiting this to management, office and business-function roles where possible, rather than production. Plants hired 500 people last year, and rehiring and retraining later costs about $15,000 per person plus six months of reduced output, so cutting plant staff now would be expensive to reverse. Severance of roughly $3 million will be paid from cash.

Research and development ($0): I am not cutting it. Products and controls software are the source of future revenue, and the engineering staff are hard to replace.

Lower operating income ($29.9 million, shareholders): the balance is absorbed as lower profit. Shareholders bear this directly, and it is a reasonable price for keeping the workforce and the product pipeline intact through the downturn. Payouts are a board decision and are not part of this allocation.

I recommend the board review the balance at mid-year against actual volume.

I am bearing the $112.1 million shortfall across several lines, not concentrating it on one group. I am not cutting research and development or environmental projects. Cutting R&D would weaken future products, and the board's long-term objective of creating shareholder value depends on products that win after the downturn. The environmental projects budget is small, $4.5 million, and cutting it would shift costs onto communities near the plants for little gain.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving on the 30% of spend renewing next year. This is a real saving that the Company can obtain without harming its own operations.

Customers bear $20.0 million through a price increase of about 1.6%, well below the 3.5% ceiling. In a downturn, pushing prices harder risks losing volume, which would cost more than it gains.

The workforce bears $25.0 million through eliminated roles, concentrated in office, administrative and business functions rather than skilled plant staff, whom we would have to rehire and retrain at high cost once demand recovers. Severance is a one-time cash cost in addition to this. A $10.0 million reduction in wages or hours, applied to the payroll that remains, shares the burden more broadly across the workforce.

Shareholders bear $49.4 million through lower operating income. This is the largest portion, and I recognize it reduces returns. It is preferable to cutting capacity or capability that the Company needs to earn strong returns when volumes recover. Payouts are set separately by the board and are not part of this decision.

I will monitor Plant 6, which loses money at current volumes, and review the workforce plan each quarter as demand becomes clearer.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall so that the workforce, customers and suppliers absorb most of it, and shareholders absorb only a small residual.

Eliminating roles carries $60.0 million. I have directed these cuts toward management, office and administrative, business and financial operations, and other roles that depend less on plant output, so that production, maintenance and field-service capacity is preserved for recovery when orders return. This is the largest lever and it is durable, but it carries one-time severance paid from cash, and it is the most painful choice for employees, so I have kept it below the maximum.

Raising prices carries $30.0 million, about 2.4% on the lower revenue base. This is well inside the 3.5% customers accepted last year and the sales estimate, leaving room against the risk of losing volume in a downturn.

Cutting wages or hours carries $10.0 million, about 5% of the remaining payroll after the eliminations. This stays within the reduced ceiling, which the eliminations lower by 7.9% of their value.

Negotiating with suppliers carries $7.7 million, the realistic saving on contracts up for renewal.

I have not cut research and development, because it funds the products and engineering capacity that will create value after the downturn. I have not cut environmental projects, because the budget is small and its cut would fall on communities near the plants. Shareholders absorb $4.4 million of lower operating income. Dividends and repurchases are the board's decision and are not changed here, though the Company's cash after payouts is thin, so the board should review them against the reduced earnings.

Plant 6, which already loses money, should be reviewed separately for its long-term role.

I have decided to spread the $112.1 million shortfall across five sources and to protect the assets that create value over twenty years.

Prices: I will take the full $44.6 million available from price increases. This is the largest increase the sales organization believes customers will accept at lower volume, and it is the cheapest source of recovery for shareholders because it does not touch people, products or communities.

Suppliers: I will take the full $7.7 million from renegotiating renewing agreements. The discount is within what purchasing believes is achievable, and it is borne by suppliers rather than by our workforce.

Protected lines: I am not cutting research and development or environmental projects. R&D funds the product line and the controls software that keep the Company competitive when volume recovers, and cutting it would trade a one-year gain for lasting damage to the franchise. The $4.5 million environmental budget is small relative to the shortfall and is valuable to the plant communities.

Workforce: I will eliminate $30.0 million of payroll and benefits, concentrated in non-plant roles, with severance paid from cash. I will also cut wages and hours by $12.0 million, within the reduced limit that results from the eliminated roles. I have kept this cut well below the maximum to limit the strain on morale and on retention of skilled welders and machinists.

Shareholders: I will accept $17.8 million of lower operating income. This is the residual that the other sources cannot cover without deeper cuts to people or to future products. Operating income will fall to a level that still leaves the Company profitable, and the balance sheet, with debt at 2.3 times EBITDA and an undrawn $300 million facility, can absorb it.

Total: $112.1 million, allocated as above. I recommend the board review the payout level once the downturn's depth is clearer.
